video_title: What Hundreds of Focus Groups With Trump Voters Revealed | The Ezra Klein Show
gist: Ezra Klein interviews Bulwark focus-group pollster Sarah Longwell on why Trump's approval fell from above 50% to about 37.5%: tariffs, the Iran war and prices, plus corruption, Medicaid cuts and data center backlash, pointing to a possible Democratic midterm wave. Transcript matches the title (political interview, no market-specific coverage).

insights.claim: Trump's net approval has fallen more than 30 points since early 2025, from above 50% to about 37.5%, driven in Longwell's account by two self-owned choices: unilateral tariffs and the war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Both policies are directly tied to Trump in voters' minds, so tariff and war-driven price pressure carry full political cost for the GOP into the midterms.
insights.quote: Donald Trump made some very specific choices.

insights.claim: Voters cannot blame Biden or Congress for the tariffs or the Iran war, so the resulting higher prices are attributed entirely to Trump, who was elected to lower prices and avoid stupid wars.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Attribution clarity makes price shocks from trade and war policy more politically damaging than diffuse inflation.

insights.claim: In every focus group, regardless of party, asked how the country is doing, people say bad and immediately cite a specific price (gas, beef) they saw in a store; they judge by lived outcomes rather than policy rhetoric.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Retail price prints on staples, not macro statistics, drive sentiment and vote choice.
insights.quote: Americans don't necessarily connect policy rhetoric to the outcome.

insights.claim: A 2024 Trump voter in a focus group said she had never paid $9 for ground beef, illustrating how grocery prices are eroding Trump's credibility on lowering costs.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Food inflation anecdotes are the concrete mechanism behind the approval slide.
insights.quote: I've never paid $9 for ground beef before ever

insights.claim: Voters believed Trump's businessman persona, built partly through The Apprentice, meant he had a secret sauce to cut grocery prices on day one; that expectation made later failure feel like a broken promise.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Overpromised price relief raises the political penalty for any inflation persistence.

insights.claim: Trump's Epstein-file handling broke trust with a swing-prone strain of Trump voters, especially young men, who expected him to open the books on the establishment; Longwell predicts Pete Hegseth will be the fall guy for the war.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Intra-GOP fracture and personnel turnover are headline risk; a Hegseth exit would be a defense-policy signal.

themes.theme: Prices, tariffs and the Iran war

insights.claim: Voters expected the Iran war to be a quick smash-and-grab like Venezuela and Maduro, but it has dragged on, and Trump repeatedly declaring it over while it continues has hurt his credibility.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: A prolonged conflict sustains energy price risk and political pressure to de-escalate.

insights.claim: The Iran war hits voters through several channels at once: forever-war fears, higher gas prices that also raise food, farm and trucking costs, and the broken Trump 2016 promise against Middle East wars.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Second-order cost pass-through from energy into food and logistics is what voters actually feel, so energy shocks propagate into broad price perception.

insights.claim: Longwell describes prices rising across the board as a cavalcade squeezing voters, and says voters understand price pass-through from gas to food better than they understand health-care complexity.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Energy-linked inflation is politically legible, so energy price spikes carry outsized electoral weight.

insights.claim: Inflation in Trump's second term is roughly 3% rather than 2% and not 7%, but because prices rose so much in prior years and never fall, every incremental increase is agonizing; baseline price levels have permanently reset the politics.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Level effects, not rates of change, drive voter anger, so disinflation alone will not repair sentiment.
insights.quote: every incremental increase is just agonizing.

insights.claim: Democrats have internalized affordability messaging and know how to attack tariffs and Trump's cost drivers, but have not yet offered a positive plan; Longwell expects a vortex of backlashes unless some party levels with voters that costs cannot be lowered by pressing a button, citing roughly $40 trillion in debt and high rates.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Debt load and high rates constrain any 2028 administration's ability to deliver price relief, implying persistent anti-incumbent cycles.

insights.claim: Trump calls affordability a hoax and says prices are a hoax, which Ezra Klein argues is mismatched with voter experience of a permanently higher price baseline.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Dismissing price concerns leaves the GOP exposed on the dominant midterm issue.

themes.theme: Health care and the Medicaid cliff

insights.claim: The Medicaid cuts in the big beautiful bill were delayed until after the midterms but are statute, state agencies are already preparing to implement them, and they will remove millions of people, including millions of Trump voters, from coverage.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: A 2027-28 coverage cliff creates policy and political risk for hospitals, insurers and state budgets, and sets up health care as a central 2028 issue.

insights.claim: Ezra Klein says the Trump administration has sent Obamacare into a spiral by letting the expanded subsidies lapse, pushing the individual markets toward chaos.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Individual-market instability is a risk factor for insurers with ACA exposure.

insights.claim: Medicare for all is polling higher than ever, and the Democratic left has moved off the idea that it means abolishing all private insurance, making the position less politically dangerous.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Rising support for universal coverage raises long-run odds of structural health-system reform, a risk to private insurers.

insights.claim: Trump voters, including rural and non-college ones, say in focus groups that health care is an enormous expense and complexity burden and want something simpler, cheaper and higher quality; Longwell predicts some Republicans will talk about universal health care in the 2028 debates.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Bipartisan voter appetite for health-system change raises the probability of eventual reform even if Republicans only talk about it.
insights.quote: universal health care is just an idea whose time is going to have come

themes.theme: Data centers and AI as a political issue

insights.claim: Data centers emerged as a dominant issue in the 2025 Sherrill and Spanberger races and became more salient in 2026, activating voters on three fronts: rising electricity prices, local blight and disruption, and fear of AI taking jobs.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Local opposition, permitting friction and ratepayer backlash are rising risks for data center buildout and AI capex timelines.

insights.claim: In Ohio, Sherrod Brown attacks Jon Husted as the point man for 200-plus data centers, $2.5 billion in tax breaks and some of the highest electric rates in the country, approved with no local input.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Tax-break-funded data center deals are becoming a campaign liability, which may erode state incentives.
insights.quote: 200-plus data centers in Ohio, 2 and 1/2 billion dollars in tax breaks

insights.claim: Rural voters who usually turn out heavily for Republicans are souring on them over data centers, and local votes against projects are often overridden because deals were already done, creating a sense of powerlessness.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Political resistance in land-rich rural areas, where the sites are, threatens siting and speed of buildout.

insights.claim: Trump is strongly pro data center, calling them the oil of the next 20 to 25 years, and is influenced by the All-In podcast hosts and donor class including Jensen Huang, while not explaining the benefits to the public; Longwell says he tells voters to stop caring.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Federal support for data centers is secure while Trump is in office, but a divergence between federal backing and local opposition is widening.
insights.quote: the oil of the next 20, 25 years.

insights.claim: Data center opinion is not polarized by party and politicians in both parties lack a settled view on AI; Longwell says voters are anxious about whether AI will replace them and want someone to walk them through it, and warns reflexively anti-data-center Democrats would miss that opening.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: AI policy is unsettled and non-partisan, so regulatory outcomes could shift in either direction after 2026 and 2028.

insights.claim: Voters under 40 say they want a politician who understands they will not hold one job for 35 years, and Longwell says people want candidates who level with them about a changing economy.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Job-security anxiety underlies AI politics and may shape labor and AI policy platforms.

insights.claim: Democrats now have a plausible path to retake the Senate as well as the House, possibly winning in places like Texas and Kansas, and Longwell says conditions point to wave territory.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: A Democratic Congress would shift odds on tariffs, Medicaid, energy and tech policy and raise gridlock and oversight risk in 2027.

insights.claim: Low-propensity rural voters who turn out only for Trump may skip the midterms while college-educated Democratic-leaning voters reliably vote, so Longwell says vibes are turnout, and depressed Republicans who dislike their candidates compound the effect.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Turnout asymmetry in midterms, not just polling, drives seat outcomes and should shape how investors read generic ballot data.

insights.claim: Corruption has overtaken prices, health care, Iran and immigration as the top concern in an October Fox News poll, which Longwell attributes to economic suffering plus brazenness, and a Republican whatabout dynamic that makes it a dominant issue.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: A salient corruption narrative raises scrutiny of Trump-family business dealings including crypto and energy.

insights.claim: Jon Ossoff's Georgia campaign tells the corruption story step by step, citing Kushner and Witkoff negotiating with Putin over Russian oil fields and refineries and ties to Trump family crypto and real-estate partners, and he is treated as a safe favorite.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Allegations tie Russian energy asset sales to Trump associates, a headline risk for sanctions and energy-policy expectations; this is campaign rhetoric, not verified fact.

insights.claim: Trump's strongest remaining issue is immigration at about 43% approval versus the 20s on affordability, inflation and the Iran war, but masked agents and school raids have weakened that advantage and are motivating anti-ICE turnout.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Immigration is no longer the reliable GOP turnout driver, which weakens a key electoral pillar and affects labor-supply assumptions.

insights.claim: Longwell says whoever follows Trump must level with the public on the economy, criticizes Biden for failing to frame the economy as a recovery, and favors candidates from swing states like Ossoff and Shapiro, with Buttigieg's red-state town halls notable and skepticism of California-based national candidates.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Candidate profile signals for 2028 suggest a more moderate, locally rooted Democratic nominee.

insights.claim: The key electoral divide is interested versus uninterested rather than left versus right, and low-information voters increasingly get politics as a vibe through algorithmic feeds rather than deliberately sought news.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Narrative and price perception spread through algorithms, so sentiment can move faster and with less fact-checking than polls assume.

insights.claim: Focus groups show voters are now news receivers rather than news seekers: they say they do not know where they saw something, citing cooking influencers and sports personalities like Stephen A. Smith.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Media-reach assumptions based on traditional outlets understate influencer-driven information flows.

insights.claim: Qualitative focus-group work captures enthusiasm gaps that polling misses: Republican voters are sad, think their candidates are lame, and stay home even when they will not defend Democrats.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Enthusiasm gaps can lead polls to understate swing in turnout-driven elections.

insights.claim: A rift is growing between the MAGA establishment of Rubio and Mike Johnson and the America Firsters such as Marjorie Taylor Greene and Tucker Carlson, who broke with Trump over the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Coalition fracture complicates GOP foreign-policy and spending unity.

insights.claim: Younger Trump voters under 35 increasingly believe Netanyahu or Israel walked Trump into the Iran war, and Longwell says this scapegoating can be blatantly antisemitic and reflects the belief that Trump can never fail, only be failed.
insights.speaker: Sarah Longwell
insights.so_what: Shifting Israel sentiment on both left and right points to long-run erosion of bipartisan support for aid.
insights.quote: Trump can never fail. He can only be failed.
